title: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions
hook: If AI accelerates AI research, how fast can that loop go? Toby Ord's answer: runaway growth is harder than the models suggest, and the neglected variable is how long one trip around the loop takes.
key_points: AI helping with AI R&D creates a feedback loop that could in principle escalate capabilities rapidly.
Ord analyses the mathematics of the most explosive cases to see what actually drives the dynamics.
Singular growth — hitting a vertical asymptote — is harder to achieve than recent economics-inspired models imply.
There's a neglected middle class: growth faster than exponential that still never reaches an asymptote.
Generation time — how long one pass around the feedback loop takes — is the pivotal parameter.
No singular growth is possible unless generation time rapidly approaches zero.
content_html: AI is already being used to help build AI. If that feedback loop is strong enough, capabilities could escalate rapidly — the "intelligence explosion." Toby Ord works through the mathematics of the most explosive possibilities, not to predict one, but to identify what actually governs the dynamics.
extra_html:
The argument

Two results. First, singular growth — capability heading toward a vertical asymptote in finite time — is harder to achieve than recent economics-inspired modelling would suggest. Second, there's an important class of trajectories that gets neglected in the binary framing: growth that is genuinely faster than exponential yet never reaches an asymptote. That middle ground matters, because "not a singularity" is often treated as "not explosive," and it isn't the same claim.

The parameter Ord elevates is generation time: how long it takes to complete one circuit of the feedback loop — AI contributes to research, that research yields a better AI, which contributes again. His conclusion is that you cannot get singular growth unless generation time rapidly approaches zero. That turns an abstract debate about returns to intelligence into a question about a concrete, arguably measurable quantity: the cycle time of AI R&D itself.

Why it matters

Explosion arguments usually turn on how much smarter each generation is. Ord's framing shifts attention to how fast generations arrive — a bottleneck that involves compute procurement, experiment runtimes, and human review, none of which shrink toward zero easily.

flashcards.prompt: What does Ord identify as the pivotal, neglected parameter in intelligence-explosion models?
flashcards.back_html: Generation time — how long it takes to go once around the AI-improves-AI feedback loop. Singular growth is impossible unless generation time rapidly approaches zero.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'neglected class' of growth rates the paper highlights?

choices.text: Growth faster than exponential that still never reaches a vertical asymptote
Growth slower than exponential but faster than linear
Oscillating growth that alternates between boom and stagnation

flashcards.explanation_html: Between ordinary exponential growth and singular growth sits an important class: super-exponential growth with no vertical asymptote.

flashcards.prompt: How does the paper's conclusion compare to recent economics-inspired modelling?

choices.text: Singular growth is harder to achieve than those models would lead you to expect
Singular growth is essentially guaranteed once AI contributes to AI R&D
It confirms those models' predictions with tighter error bars

flashcards.explanation_html: Ord shows that reaching a vertical asymptote is harder than recent economics-inspired modelling suggests.
